passage: In the small room at the family counselling centre, Uday and Harsha sat with a sheet of paper between them, writing their rules in two colours. Harsha read them out. "One: pauses are allowed, but you say when you're coming back. Two: nobody is left guessing for more than a day." Uday added, "Three: if either of us goes quiet for days again, or uses silence to get our way, we book another session here. No arguing about it." The counsellor nodded. "That last one matters. Silence that keeps coming back, or that's used to control, is worth getting help for." Harsha folded the paper and put it in her bag. "Fridge door," she said. Uday smiled. "Next to the milk bill."

qa.q: Where will the paper go?
qa.a: On the fridge door, next to the milk bill.

qa.q: What does Uday's smile at the end suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Uday feels hopeful and at ease about the agreement they have made together.

qa.q: Why is rule three a wise addition?
qa.a: It plans ahead: if silence becomes long or controlling again, they agree to seek the counsellor's help rather than argue about it.

qa.q: How might the rule about never being left guessing help Harsha?
qa.a: Harsha no longer has to wonder whether a silence means rejection, since every pause comes with a return time.

grounding: Shows a couple agreeing that pauses need a return time, no one is left guessing, and repeated or controlling silence means going back to a counsellor.

passage:
Pranav,
I'm writing down what we agreed last night, so neither of us "remembers it differently" in a month.
1. Pauses are allowed. Whoever needs one says how long, and comes back when they said.
2. Nobody gets left wondering. Even "still upset, will talk after dinner" counts.
3. No deleting messages. If you type "I miss you", send it. (Yes, I know about that. You told me.)
4. If we slip back into days of silence, or if either of us starts using quiet to win, we find a counsellor. Not as a punishment. As help.
I'm sticking this on the bathroom mirror. I love you, even when the house is quiet.
Ishita

qa.q: Where is Ishita sticking the letter?
qa.a: Ishita is sticking it on the bathroom mirror.

qa.q: Why does Ishita want the agreement written down?
qa.a: Ishita worries that in a month one of them might "remember it differently", so writing it down makes it stick.

qa.q: What does rule four add that the others don't?
qa.a: It sets a clear point for getting outside help if long or controlling silences return, framed as help rather than punishment.

qa.q: How might Pranav feel reading rule three?
qa.a: Pranav may feel a little exposed but also relieved that the deleted "I miss you" is now welcome to be sent. 🙂

grounding: Shows a couple writing new rules: pauses with a return time, nobody left guessing, and a counsellor if silence becomes continual or controlling.

passage:
People ask me and Manjula how we fight now. I'm Ritu. We've lived together four years, and the first two were full of silent days.
So we made two rules, and we wrote them on the fridge.
Rule one: you're allowed to pause. But you have to say when you'll come back. "I need till after dinner." "Give me an hour." No open-ended silence.
Rule two: nobody gets left guessing. If you're upset, you say so, even if you can't say why yet.
And we agreed on one more thing: if either of us ever starts using silence to control the other, again and again, we go and see a counsellor. No shame in it. That's what it's for.

qa.q: Where did Ritu and Manjula write their rules?
qa.a: On the fridge.

qa.q: What does Ritu seem to feel now about how they handle conflict?
qa.a: Ritu seems relieved and confident, proud of the rules that replaced their silent days.

qa.q: What makes their new rules work?
qa.a: Pauses are allowed only with a return time, and no one is left guessing, so silence becomes a signal rather than a weapon.

qa.q: How might Manjula experience a pause under the new rules?
qa.a: Manjula can wait calmly, knowing exactly when Ritu will come back, instead of fearing being shut out.

grounding: A young adult describes new rules: pauses allowed with a return time, no one left guessing, and a counsellor if silence becomes controlling.

passage:
I live across the corridor from Darshan and Pooja. For a year, their flat went silent for days at a time. I'd see Pooja on the stairs, eyes red, and her husband Darshan coming home late and saying nothing.
Then something changed. Last month I heard them argue, and then I heard Darshan say, clearly, "I need a break. I'll be back at eight." At eight, their door opened and closed. I heard them talking, low voices, for a long time.
Later Pooja told me they'd been seeing a counsellor. They had a list on their fridge now: "Pause with a time. Never leave the other guessing."
I don't know everything that goes on in their home. But it's been a long time since I saw Pooja crying on the stairs.

qa.q: What time did Darshan say he would be back?
qa.a: At eight.

qa.q: What was Pooja likely feeling during the year of silent days?
qa.a: She seemed hurt and lonely, often red-eyed on the stairs.

qa.q: What helped the couple change?
qa.a: They saw a counsellor and made rules: pause only with a return time and never leave the other guessing.

qa.q: What might Darshan experience now when he asks for a break?
qa.a: He can take the space he needs without guilt, because naming a return time means Pooja is not left guessing.

grounding: A neighbour observes a couple move from long silences to pauses with a return time, after seeing a counsellor and agreeing new rules.

passage:
Friday: Indu and Vasudha had their worst fight in months, about Vasudha's night shifts. Vasudha went silent for the whole weekend, as she often did.
Monday: They sat with the counsellor Indu had found. Indu said, "I never know if the silence is ending in an hour or a week." The counsellor asked them to agree on what a fair pause looks like. They settled on two rules: pauses are okay if you say when you'll be back, and nobody is left guessing.
Thursday: A smaller argument. Vasudha said, "I'm too upset. I'll come find you at nine." At nine, she knocked on Indu's door. Indu found she was not scared this time.

qa.q: What did Vasudha say during Thursday's argument?
qa.a: "I'm too upset. I'll come find you at nine."

qa.q: What was Indu feeling on Thursday when Vasudha asked for a pause?
qa.a: Indu felt calm and not scared, because this time she knew when Vasudha would come back.

qa.q: What turning point helped Indu and Vasudha?
qa.a: Seeing a counsellor and agreeing that pauses need a return time and no one is left guessing changed silence from a threat into a signal.

qa.q: What was Vasudha experiencing when she knocked on the door at nine?
qa.a: She was likely still upset but calmer, and able to keep her promise to come back.

grounding: Over a week, a couple see a counsellor and agree that pauses need a return time and no one is left guessing, and a small fight goes better.

passage:
Uday, you asked why your Dilnaz Khala and your Khalu never have those long silent fights anymore. We used to, you know. Terrible ones.

In our first year married, when we fought, he would go silent for two, three days. I never knew when it would end. I'd lie awake guessing.

One evening we sat down and made rules, like children making a game. Rule one: anyone can say "I need a break." Rule two: you must say when you'll come back. "One hour." "Tomorrow morning." Rule three: nobody is left guessing, ever.

The first time he said "back at nine," I watched the clock. At nine, he came.

I'll tell you one more thing, beta. If someone's silence never ends and is used to control you, rules aren't enough. Then you go to a counsellor. We nearly did. There's no shame in it.

qa.q: What was rule two?
qa.a: Rule two was that you must say when you'll come back.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling during those early two- and three-day silences?
qa.a: She felt anxious and uncertain, lying awake guessing because she never knew when the silence would end.

qa.q: What was the choice inside the story that changed their fights?
qa.a: Sitting down together to make rules, so pauses always had a return time and nobody was left guessing.

qa.q: How might Khalu have felt the first time he said 'back at nine' and kept it?
qa.a: Khalu probably felt relieved and trusted, able to take the break he needed without it hurting his wife.

grounding: An elder recalls agreeing that pauses need a return time and no one is left guessing, and that a counsellor helps if silence controls.
